history: Latin had two whites: albus, a dull white, and candidus, a bright one. French kept neither. Both were pushed out by a Germanic word, *blank, which came straight into the Latin spoken in Gaul, and into Italian and Catalan too: Italian bianco, Catalan blanc. The TLFi compares Old English blanca and Old Norse blakkr, ‘pale’, a word used especially of horses. Blanc is one of the earliest French words on record: the Passion of Clermont, from the end of the 10th century, speaks of blanc vestimenz, ‘white clothes’. Blanc belongs with bleu, blond, brun and gris, the colour words French took from Germanic. Watch the feminine: blanche, with ch, as in une nuit blanche, ‘a sleepless night’.
historyEinfach: Blanc is not a Latin word. The Latin words for ‘white’ were albus and candidus, but people stopped using them. They took a Germanic word, blank. Italian bianco is the same word. The feminine form is blanche: une maison blanche. Une nuit blanche, ‘a white night’, is a night without sleep.

elsewhere.text: Italian took the same Germanic word, so French blanc and Italian bianco are twins, while the Latin albus survives in neither as the everyday word.
